transcript.content: Hello, it’s nice to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, hello there, Doctor. I... I came down here today because, see, the men at the domino table have been giving me these little messages. Just meant for me. And sometimes the radio announcer does it too, warning me to be careful. 

My wife, she says it’s just talk, but... well, she don't listen to the radio like I do. We got this old Zenith radio, you know, the big wooden kind? Bought it back in... oh, must've been '72 or '73. Still works real good. Catches the AM stations clear as a bell, especially on a cold morning. I used to tinker with radios a bit. Never had the proper schooling for it, you know, I had to leave school in the eighth grade to help my daddy out on the farm. But you learn by doing. 

Anyway, she was making her beef stew yesterday—she always puts too much pepper in it now, her taster's going—and I told her to listen to the man on the broadcast, but she just stirred the pot and told me it's nonsense. But I know they're warning me, Doctor. I know what I hear.
How long have you been receiving these messages from the domino players and the radio announcer?

Let me think on that... it must be, oh, about nine months now. On and off, you know. It started right around the time the transmission went out on my grandson Jimmy's truck. He brought it over to the house, thinking I could fix it. I told him I ain't a mechanic, I just tinker with small engines. Lawnmowers, mostly. Those old Briggs and Stratton engines, they are just the easiest things to work on. You just clean the carburetor out with a little spray and they fire right up on the first pull. Used to do all the neighbors' mowers for a few dollars. 

Anyway, Jimmy ended up having to tow his truck to that shop down on Elm Street. Cost him a pretty penny, too. Young folks today, they just don't know how to save their money. Buy a cup of coffee for five dollars when you can make a whole pot at home for pennies. But yes sir, that is when I first started noticing the special messages and the voices. Right around nine months ago. Give or take.
Have you used any recreational drugs?

Recreational drugs? Oh, Lord, no. Never touched anything like that in my life. I don't even smoke cigarettes anymore. Gave those up back in... well, it was the year they put the new roof on the Methodist church. Used to smoke Pall Malls, the unfiltered ones. My daddy smoked them, and I guess I just picked up the habit. 

But no, no drugs. I take my blood pressure pill, and a little aspirin for my joints when the weather turns wet. You know, when that rain comes off the gulf, my left knee aches like nobody's business. I injured it falling off a tractor when I was nineteen. We were pulling stumps out of the lower pasture, and the chain snapped. Whipped right back and took my legs out from under me. I was lucky it didn't take my head off, honestly. The local doctor—old Dr. Henderson, he's passed on now, bless his soul—he wrapped it up real tight with some kind of liniment that smelled like wintergreen and horse sweat. Told me to stay off it for a month. Try telling a farmer to stay off his feet for a month! 

But anyway, no sir, I don't mess with any of those illegal things. Just my regular medicine from the pharmacy.
How have these messages and voices affected your ability to manage your usual daily activities?

Well, I suppose it has changed my routine some. Like... well, I've missed a few of my choir rehearsals lately. I sing bass down at the Methodist church. Been singing there since... oh, must be fifty years now. We used to have Mrs. Gable directing, and she played the piano so hard she'd bounce right up off the bench! Now they got this young fella who wants us singing all these new songs. I keep telling him, you just can't beat "How Great Thou Art." Nothing sounds better than a full choir on that chorus. But anyway, I just haven't been going because it's hard to focus on the music with everything else going on. 

And my garden, well... I've let parts of it just go to weed this year. I usually grow a big patch of tomatoes. Those Big Boy tomatoes, you know? Best thing in the world is a fresh tomato sandwich with a little mayonnaise and black pepper on soft white bread. My daddy taught me to bury crushed eggshells under the roots to stop the bottoms from rotting out. Works like a charm. It's the calcium, I reckon. But I just haven't had the mind to get out there in the dirt and tend to it all like I should. 

And the domino games... well, I guess I made things a bit uncomfortable down at the tables. When I started hearing the men sending me those little warnings, I'd call them out on it, and... well, it got real tense. So I just don't join in the games like I used to. Earl still waves when I walk by, but I just keep on walking. He always was a cheat at dominoes anyway, holding onto that double-six till the very end... but no, I don't sit with them much anymore.
Have you noticed any recent problems with your memory or thinking?

Memory? No, no, I don't think so. My mind's still as sharp as a tack, far as I can tell. I remember things just fine. Like the other day, I was trying to remember the name of that fella who used to run the hardware store down on Main Street. Not the new one with the bright orange sign, but the old one, before the big storm took the roof off. You know the storm I'm talking about? Back in '78, I think it was. Blew the old oak tree right over onto Mrs. Higgins' porch. She was so upset about that tree. Said her grandfather planted it when he came back from the war. 

Anyway, the hardware store fella... his name was Arthur! Arthur Pendelton. Sold me my first set of socket wrenches. Heavy things, real steel, not like the cheap metal they use nowadays. You'd strip a bolt with these new ones before you even got it tight. Arthur always had a jar of peppermint candies on the counter for the kids. The ones with the red stripes. I used to get one every time my daddy went in for nails. We were building a new chicken coop out back because the old one got into by a fox. Sneaky things, foxes. You gotta bury the chicken wire at least a foot down or they'll just dig right under it. 

But no, my memory is just fine. I haven't noticed any trouble with it at all.
How old are you?

Well, I'm eighty-four years old now. Eighty-four. Sometimes I can hardly believe it myself. Seems like just yesterday I was turning sixty and thinking that was old! We had a big barbecue for my sixtieth. Roasted a whole pig right out there in the yard. My brother-in-law, Thomas—he was married to my sister Sarah, God rest her soul—he built this cinderblock pit just for the occasion. Took him three days to get the draft right on that thing. He was always tinkering with stuff like that. Used to work down at the railyard before they shut it down in the nineties. 

Anyway, that pig was something else. We had to baste it with a mop! Just a regular cotton mop dipped in a bucket of vinegar and pepper sauce. Best barbecue I ever had. People still talk about it sometimes, the ones that are left around here. But yeah, eighty-four. Born in the spring, right around the time the bluebonnets start coming up along the highway. You ever notice how they always grow thickest right there on the shoulder? I always thought it was the wind from the cars blowing the seeds around, but who knows.
Did these experiences begin after any significant change in your health?

Well, let's see... a change in my health? No, my health's been about the same. But I can tell you exactly when all this started. It's been about a year and five months now. Started right after my good friend Charlie passed away. Oh, Charlie... we knew each other since we were knee-high to a grasshopper. We used to go fishing down at Miller's Pond every single Saturday, rain or shine. He had this old aluminum johnboat that leaked just a little bit right near the transom. Not enough to sink you, but you had to keep a coffee tin handy to bail it out every hour or so. 

He always swore by those jitterbug lures. The green ones with the little yellow spots. Said the bass couldn't resist the sound they made popping across the top of the water. I always preferred a simple worm and bobber myself. There's something peaceful about just watching that red and white plastic bobbing out there, waiting for it to dip under. We'd sit out there for hours, drinking RC Cola and eating those little Debbie oatmeal cream pies. You know the ones? They used to be a lot bigger back in the day. Everything's getting smaller now, it seems. Even the candy bars at the checkout line. 

But yeah, it was right after Charlie's funeral that all this started up. About a year and five months ago. We buried him out at the Restland Cemetery, right near that big weeping willow tree. Beautiful spot, really. The shade keeps the grass nice and green all summer long.
Has a doctor ever told you that you have a neurological or brain condition?

A brain condition? No, no sir. Never had any doctor tell me anything like that. I mean, old Doc Evans—he was the one who delivered half the county, you know—he did have to patch up my head once. But that was just a cut. Must've been... oh, the summer of '82, I reckon. I was working on the old John Deere combine out in the field. The green ones, you know? Not the big fancy machines they have now with the air-conditioned cabs and the satellite radios. Just a metal seat that'd burn the hide right off you if you left it sitting in the sun too long. You had to throw a burlap sack over it just to sit down. 

Anyway, I slipped off the ladder and whacked my head right on the hitch. Bled like a stuck pig. Head wounds always do, they say. Doc Evans put about eight stitches right here above my ear. He used this thick black thread, looked just like heavy-test fishing line. He always smelled like cherry pipe tobacco and rubbing alcohol, Doc Evans did. He'd smoke a corn cob pipe right there in the examination room while he was sewing you up! Can you imagine that today? They'd probably shut the whole clinic down for that now. But no, he never said nothing about my actual brain being bad. Just told me to keep the stitches clean and stay out of the midday sun for a spell.
Have you recently become confused about where you are?

Confused about where I am? No, I always know where I'm at. I've lived in this county my whole life, so there ain't a road or a dirt path I don't recognize. Even when they put in that new bypass over by the old Miller farm—you know the one, where they tore down that beautiful red barn? Such a shame, too. That barn was built back in the twenties. They used real wooden pegs instead of nails for the main beams. My daddy used to say a barn built with pegs would sway in a tornado but it wouldn't snap. 

I remember when we used to go out there to pick up hay. We'd stack those square bales so high on the flatbed you'd think the whole truck was gonna tip over going around a bend. You had to wear long sleeves, even in August, or that hay would scratch your arms up something awful. And the dust! You'd be sneezing for two days straight after hauling hay. We'd always stop at the filling station on the way back and get a cold bottle of Nehi Grape. Nothing tasted better than that cold grape soda after sweating in a hayfield all afternoon. But no, I don't get confused about where I am. I know exactly where I am.
Has your wife noticed any decline in your memory recently?

My memory? No, she hasn't said anything about my memory slipping. Martha's usually pretty quick to point out if I forget something, like taking out the trash on Tuesday mornings. You know, the sanitation department changed their route a few years back. Used to be they'd come around on Thursdays, right about the time the mailman, Mr. Henderson, would drop off the post. 

Mr. Henderson was a real character. He had this little white mail truck with the steering wheel on the wrong side. He'd always leave a milk bone in the mailbox for our old golden retriever, Buster. Best dog we ever had, Buster was. We found him wandering near the old train tracks on the edge of town, just a skinny little pup. Took him in, fed him some leftover meatloaf, and he never left our side after that. He loved riding in the back of my pickup truck, just letting his ears flap in the wind. We had a '78 Ford F-150 back then. Two-tone, brown and tan. Had a manual transmission with the shifter right there on the steering column. Three on the tree, they called it. You don't see those much anymore. Everybody wants an automatic now, so they can hold their coffee in one hand and their telephone in the other while they drive. But no, Martha hasn't mentioned anything about my memory.
Has a doctor found any medical or neurological condition that could explain these experiences?

No, no doctor has ever said anything like that. They haven't found any medical reason for what I go through. I mean, they did all sorts of blood tests a while back, taking vials and vials of it. The nurse who drew my blood, she was a sweet girl. Had hair the color of spun gold, just like my niece Sarah. 

Sarah used to come visit us every summer when she was little. We'd take her down to the creek to catch crawdads. You had to tie a piece of bacon to a string and just dangle it in the water, wait for them to pinch it. Then you'd scoop 'em up real quick with a net. We'd keep 'em in a galvanized bucket for a while, just to watch 'em, then toss 'em back. Sarah loved that. She's all grown up now, of course. Moved out to Seattle, works for one of those big computer companies. Sends us a Christmas card every year with a picture of her and her husband. They got a nice-looking house, big windows. But no, the doctors haven't found any physical sickness that would cause all this.
Do you hear voices speaking to you when you are alone and there is no radio or other person nearby?

Voices? Well, yes, sometimes I do. Some afternoons, when the house is real quiet and Martha's out at her garden club, I hear my old friend Jimmy. He'll call my name from the front porch, or I'll hear him humming one of those old choir songs, clear as day, like he's standing right there next to me. 

Jimmy had a beautiful baritone voice, you know. We used to sing in the church choir together back at First Methodist. The choir director, Mrs. Gable, she was a strict woman. Always wore these floral dresses with a lace collar and had her hair pinned up tight. If you missed a note, she'd tap her baton on the music stand so hard you'd think she was gonna snap it in two. But she knew how to get a good sound out of us. We did a Christmas cantata back in '65 that folks talked about for years. Jimmy had the solo on "O Holy Night." He hit that high note at the end and I swear the stained glass windows rattled just a little bit. 

Those windows were something else, too. They were imported all the way from Italy when the church was built. Had the whole story of the Good Samaritan in the big one facing the street. I remember sitting in the pew as a boy, just watching the sunlight come through that red glass in the Samaritan's robe. It would cast this pink glow right across the wooden pews. They don't make glass like that anymore, all hand-blown and pieced together with lead. Takes a real craftsman to do that kind of work. But yes, I hear Jimmy humming sometimes when I'm all alone.

Aside from the messages and voices, have you noticed yourself becoming unusually disorganized—for example, having trouble keeping your thoughts connected or behaving in ways that seem confusing to others?

Disorganized? Well, I don't know if I'd call it that, but the fellas down at the lodge have been giving me a hard time lately. We play dominoes every Thursday afternoon, have for years. Lately, I guess I've been... well, I'll start tapping the tiles, you know? Just tapping them in this specific pattern, over and over. And sometimes I'll hold my hand up, kind of like a crossing guard stopping traffic, right in the middle of a hand. The guys will be telling me, "Come on, just play your tile," but I just... I have to do it that way. 

We play on this old felt-covered table that used to belong to Arthur Pendelton. Arthur was a character. He owned the hardware store on Main Street, the one that burned down back in '92. Terribly sad thing, that fire. Started in the back room where they kept the paint thinner. The fire department was there for hours, spraying water all over the place. The chief back then was a big burly fella named O'Malley. He had this magnificent mustache, curled right up at the ends. Used wax on it every morning, he told me once. He was always chewing on an unlit cigar, too. Said he promised his wife he'd quit smoking, so he just chewed on 'em instead. I don't know if that's any better for you, honestly. But yeah, the dominoes... the fellas get a little confused when I start tapping and holding my hand up like that.
Do you hear voices even when you are not thinking about the messages from the domino players or the radio?

Well, I suppose I do... yes. The voices don't really care what I'm thinking about. I could be out on the porch, just watching the cars go by, not thinking about the dominoes or the radio at all, and Jimmy will still start humming. 

I was sitting out there just yesterday, actually. Watching Mr. Henderson's boy mow the lawn across the street. He uses one of those old push mowers, the kind with the spinning blades that go snick-snick-snick. It's good exercise for a boy his age. I had one just like it when I was a teenager. Used to cut grass all over the neighborhood for fifty cents a yard. Saved up enough to buy myself a genuine leather baseball mitt. The smell of that leather... there's nothing quite like it. I used to rub neat's-foot oil into it every night to keep it soft. Kept it under my mattress so it would form a perfect pocket. Played third base for the county league. We had a game against the boys from Oakhaven once, and I caught a line drive right down the third-base line that would've taken my head off if I hadn't put my glove up in time. The crowd went wild. My father was in the stands, wearing his good Sunday hat... but, what was I saying? Oh, right. No, the voices just come when they please, regardless of what's on my mind.
Have people told you recently that your speech is difficult to follow or that your thoughts seem to jump from one subject to another?

Well, my daughter Martha mentioned something about that just the other morning over breakfast. She said she couldn't keep up with what I was saying. But it's just... my mind runs from the choir to baseball to repairs to my friend Jimmy and back again so fast that I cannot hold one thought long enough to explain it right. 

Speaking of repairs, I was looking at the hinges on our screen door yesterday and they are getting awful rusty. You have to keep those oiled or they'll squeak every time the wind blows. My father used to keep a little can of 3-in-One oil on the top shelf in the mudroom just for things like that. That mudroom always smelled like wet wool and machine oil. We had this big old sheepdog named Barnaby who used to sleep out there on an old braided rug. Best dog you could ever ask for, though he had a terrible habit of chasing the mailman. 

The mail carrier back then was a fella named Mr. Higgins. He wore this smart little gray uniform with a cap, and he always kept a pocketful of dog biscuits to keep Barnaby at bay. Higgins had a bit of a limp from the war, you know. Served over in the Pacific. He brought back a real Japanese compass and showed it to me once when I was a boy... but, yes, I suppose my thoughts do jump around a bit too fast for folks to follow sometimes.
Have you had trouble managing tasks you used to handle independently, such as paying bills, taking medications, or getting dressed?

Well, managing things... I suppose some things have slipped a bit. I haven't been going to choir rehearsals lately, which is a shame. And I've let parts of my garden go to weed. Plus, like I said, I've made the domino games uncomfortable enough that I just don't join in like I used to. 

I used to grow the most beautiful prize-winning tomatoes in that garden. Big, juicy Beefsteaks. My wife, Lord rest her soul, used to make the most wonderful tomato preserves. People think tomato preserves sound strange, but you put a little ginger and lemon in there, and it's just delightful on a piece of toast. We had this old toaster, a heavy chrome thing that you had to flip the sides down to turn the bread. You had to watch it like a hawk or it would burn your toast to a crisp. My brother Henry burned a piece so bad once, it set off the smoke alarm and the fire department came. It wasn't O'Malley that time, though, it was a younger fellow... but yes, I guess I haven't been keeping up with things as well as I should.
Who currently manages the household bills, and has that responsibility changed from how it was handled before these symptoms began?

Well, the bills... Martha handles all of that now. My daughter, Martha. She took over the checkbook a few months back. I used to do it all myself, you know. Every Friday evening, I'd sit down at the kitchen table with my ledger and a good, sharp pencil. 

I always liked the yellow Ticonderoga pencils. The eraser on those is just the right kind of rubber, doesn't smudge the paper when you make a mistake. My father taught me to keep my pencils sharp with a pocketknife. He had this little bone-handled Case knife he carried everywhere. Used it to whittle little wooden whistles out of willow branches for me and Henry when we were boys. You have to get the willow in the spring when the sap is running, or the bark won't slip off right to make the air chamber. Henry was always better at making them than I was. He could get a real high, clear note out of his, while mine always sounded a bit airy. Henry ended up playing the trumpet in the high school marching band, actually. They had these maroon uniforms with gold braiding on the shoulders. He looked so sharp marching down Main Street in the Fourth of July parade... but, oh, what were we talking about? The bills. Yes, Martha pays them now. I just couldn't keep the numbers straight anymore.
Before you began hearing voices and receiving messages, had you already been having a gradual decline in your memory or ability to manage everyday tasks?

Well, no, not really. Before all that business with the voices and the messages started, I was doing just fine. My memory was sharp as a tack. I remember the exact day the messages started coming through the radio, actually. We have this little silver radio in the kitchen. Not like the old Philco we had when I was a boy. Now that was a real radio. Beautiful wooden cabinet, took up half the parlor. My father bought it back in... oh, must have been 1938 or so. 

We used to sit around it on Sunday nights and listen to Jack Benny. He was such a funny man. We'd have popcorn, too. Mother would pop it right on the stove in a heavy cast-iron skillet with a bit of bacon grease. You just don't get popcorn that tastes like that from those microwave bags they have nowadays. The bags always leave a funny waxy coating on the roof of your mouth. Martha buys those bags for her kids, and I tell her, 'Martha, just use a pan!' But everybody is in such a rush these days. Rush, rush, rush... wait, what was it you asked me? Did you want to know about the radio?
Before the past year or so, had you ever heard voices or believed that other people were sending you special messages?

Well, no, never before. It's really just been happening on and off for about 9 months now. Nine months... so that means it started right around the end of the summer. We had a terrible heatwave late last August, just baked the ground solid. It was so hot the tar on the county roads was getting soft and sticking to the tires of my old Ford pickup. 

That truck was a 1974 F-150, powder blue. Best vehicle I ever owned. Had a three-on-the-tree manual transmission. You don't see those anymore. Kids today wouldn't know how to shift a gear if their lives depended on it. Everything is automatic now. Automatic cars, automatic coffee makers... I remember when you had to percolate coffee on the stove. It made that wonderful bubbling sound, and the whole house would smell like roasting beans. My mother used to buy the Eight O'Clock coffee from the A&P store down the road. They'd grind it right there at the checkout counter, and the cashier, Mrs. Gable, she always gave me a piece of peppermint candy. The bag of coffee had this little metal tie at the top to keep it fresh, and I used to save those ties to fix things around the house... but, what did you ask me? Did you want to know about the truck? Oh, the voices. Yes, no, it hasn't been forever. Just the last nine months or so.
Has your daughter noticed that you forget recent events or conversations?

Well, no, I don't think Martha's said anything about me forgetting things. We talk every morning, actually. She calls me right at eight o'clock when she's driving the kids to school. She's got this big minivan now, one of those ones where the doors slide open by themselves if you just push a button on the keys. 

I don't know how I feel about all these buttons and computers in cars. Back when I got my first car, it was a 1952 Chevrolet Bel Air. Had this beautiful chrome grille that looked like a big smile. I used to spend every Saturday morning out in the driveway, just polishing that chrome until you could see your reflection in it clear as day. Used Turtle Wax, the kind that came in the little green tub. You had to rub it on, let it dry to a haze, and then buff it off with a soft cloth. I always used my old flannel shirts for buffing once they got too threadbare to wear. They were the best for not scratching the paint. My wife, Helen, God rest her soul, she used to get so mad at me because I'd be out there fussing with the car instead of helping her in the garden. She grew the most beautiful tomatoes, big red Beefsteaks. We'd slice them thick, put a little salt and pepper on them, and eat them right on white bread with mayonnaise... but, oh, what was it you were asking? Did you want to know about the tomatoes? No, wait... about Martha? Yeah, she hasn't mentioned me forgetting things.

doctor.intent: Understand the patient's main concern
doctor.question: Hello, it’s nice to meet you. What brings you in today?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: Doctor, I came because the men at the domino table and sometimes the radio announcer give little messages meant for me, and even when my wife says it is just talk, I know they are warning me to be careful.
target_item.reason: This is the first reply of the consultation, so I must return the chief complaint symptom code, which is S019.

patient.answer:
Well, hello there, Doctor. I... I came down here today because, see, the men at the domino table have been giving me these little messages. Just meant for me. And sometimes the radio announcer does it too, warning me to be careful. 

My wife, she says it’s just talk, but... well, she don't listen to the radio like I do. We got this old Zenith radio, you know, the big wooden kind? Bought it back in... oh, must've been '72 or '73. Still works real good. Catches the AM stations clear as a bell, especially on a cold morning. I used to tinker with radios a bit. Never had the proper schooling for it, you know, I had to leave school in the eighth grade to help my daddy out on the farm. But you learn by doing. 

Anyway, she was making her beef stew yesterday—she always puts too much pepper in it now, her taster's going—and I told her to listen to the man on the broadcast, but she just stirred the pot and told me it's nonsense. But I know they're warning me, Doctor. I know what I hear.

inference.note: Persecutory/referential beliefs and possible auditory hallucinations suggest a psychotic-spectrum disorder; duration, functional decline, mood symptoms, substance exposure, and medical causes remain unclear.

doctor.intent: Determine the duration of the psychotic symptoms
doctor.question: How long have you been receiving these messages from the domino players and the radio announcer?

target_item.name: Psychotic Symptoms Duration
target_item.manifestation: The voices and special messages have been happening on and off for about 9 months now.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking 'How long have you been receiving these messages...' which directly pertains to the duration of the delusions (psychotic symptoms).

patient.answer:
Let me think on that... it must be, oh, about nine months now. On and off, you know. It started right around the time the transmission went out on my grandson Jimmy's truck. He brought it over to the house, thinking I could fix it. I told him I ain't a mechanic, I just tinker with small engines. Lawnmowers, mostly. Those old Briggs and Stratton engines, they are just the easiest things to work on. You just clean the carburetor out with a little spray and they fire right up on the first pull. Used to do all the neighbors' mowers for a few dollars. 

Anyway, Jimmy ended up having to tow his truck to that shop down on Elm Street. Cost him a pretty penny, too. Young folks today, they just don't know how to save their money. Buy a cup of coffee for five dollars when you can make a whole pot at home for pennies. But yes sir, that is when I first started noticing the special messages and the voices. Right around nine months ago. Give or take.

inference.note: Nine months of persistent referential messages and voices makes F23 less likely because symptoms exceed one month; the remaining possibilities require assessment of broader psychotic symptoms, medical causes, and substance exposure.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the psychotic symptoms could be substance-induced
doctor.question: Have you used any recreational drugs?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the use of recreational drugs, which is not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Recreational drugs? Oh, Lord, no. Never touched anything like that in my life. I don't even smoke cigarettes anymore. Gave those up back in... well, it was the year they put the new roof on the Methodist church. Used to smoke Pall Malls, the unfiltered ones. My daddy smoked them, and I guess I just picked up the habit. 

But no, no drugs. I take my blood pressure pill, and a little aspirin for my joints when the weather turns wet. You know, when that rain comes off the gulf, my left knee aches like nobody's business. I injured it falling off a tractor when I was nineteen. We were pulling stumps out of the lower pasture, and the chain snapped. Whipped right back and took my legs out from under me. I was lucky it didn't take my head off, honestly. The local doctor—old Dr. Henderson, he's passed on now, bless his soul—he wrapped it up real tight with some kind of liniment that smelled like wintergreen and horse sweat. Told me to stay off it for a month. Try telling a farmer to stay off his feet for a month! 

But anyway, no sir, I don't mess with any of those illegal things. Just my regular medicine from the pharmacy.

inference.note: Persistent referential and auditory psychotic symptoms are established; the patient denies recreational drug use, making F19.959 less likely. Medical/neurologic causes remain to be assessed.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the psychotic experiences have caused significant decline in daily functioning, which helps distinguish delusional disorder from schizophrenia-spectrum illness.
doctor.question: How have these messages and voices affected your ability to manage your usual daily activities?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I have missed choir rehearsals, let parts of my garden go, and made the domino games uncomfortable enough that I do not join like I used to.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how the symptoms have affected my ability to manage my usual daily activities, which corresponds directly to the functional impairment criterion.

patient.answer:
Well, I suppose it has changed my routine some. Like... well, I've missed a few of my choir rehearsals lately. I sing bass down at the Methodist church. Been singing there since... oh, must be fifty years now. We used to have Mrs. Gable directing, and she played the piano so hard she'd bounce right up off the bench! Now they got this young fella who wants us singing all these new songs. I keep telling him, you just can't beat "How Great Thou Art." Nothing sounds better than a full choir on that chorus. But anyway, I just haven't been going because it's hard to focus on the music with everything else going on. 

And my garden, well... I've let parts of it just go to weed this year. I usually grow a big patch of tomatoes. Those Big Boy tomatoes, you know? Best thing in the world is a fresh tomato sandwich with a little mayonnaise and black pepper on soft white bread. My daddy taught me to bury crushed eggshells under the roots to stop the bottoms from rotting out. Works like a charm. It's the calcium, I reckon. But I just haven't had the mind to get out there in the dirt and tend to it all like I should. 

And the domino games... well, I guess I made things a bit uncomfortable down at the tables. When I started hearing the men sending me those little warnings, I'd call them out on it, and... well, it got real tense. So I just don't join in the games like I used to. Earl still waves when I walk by, but I just keep on walking. He always was a cheat at dominoes anyway, holding onto that double-six till the very end... but no, I don't sit with them much anymore.

doctor.intent: Assess for cognitive decline suggesting a psychotic disorder due to a medical or neurocognitive condition
doctor.question: Have you noticed any recent problems with your memory or thinking?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about cognitive problems such as memory loss or general issues with thinking, which are not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Memory? No, no, I don't think so. My mind's still as sharp as a tack, far as I can tell. I remember things just fine. Like the other day, I was trying to remember the name of that fella who used to run the hardware store down on Main Street. Not the new one with the bright orange sign, but the old one, before the big storm took the roof off. You know the storm I'm talking about? Back in '78, I think it was. Blew the old oak tree right over onto Mrs. Higgins' porch. She was so upset about that tree. Said her grandfather planted it when he came back from the war. 

Anyway, the hardware store fella... his name was Arthur! Arthur Pendelton. Sold me my first set of socket wrenches. Heavy things, real steel, not like the cheap metal they use nowadays. You'd strip a bolt with these new ones before you even got it tight. Arthur always had a jar of peppermint candies on the counter for the kids. The ones with the red stripes. I used to get one every time my daddy went in for nails. We were building a new chicken coop out back because the old one got into by a fox. Sneaky things, foxes. You gotta bury the chicken wire at least a foot down or they'll just dig right under it. 

But no, my memory is just fine. I haven't noticed any trouble with it at all.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the late-onset psychosis is more suggestive of a secondary medical condition
doctor.question: How old are you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking for my age, which is a demographic detail and not a psychiatric symptom in my profile.

patient.answer:
Well, I'm eighty-four years old now. Eighty-four. Sometimes I can hardly believe it myself. Seems like just yesterday I was turning sixty and thinking that was old! We had a big barbecue for my sixtieth. Roasted a whole pig right out there in the yard. My brother-in-law, Thomas—he was married to my sister Sarah, God rest her soul—he built this cinderblock pit just for the occasion. Took him three days to get the draft right on that thing. He was always tinkering with stuff like that. Used to work down at the railyard before they shut it down in the nineties. 

Anyway, that pig was something else. We had to baste it with a mop! Just a regular cotton mop dipped in a bucket of vinegar and pepper sauce. Best barbecue I ever had. People still talk about it sometimes, the ones that are left around here. But yeah, eighty-four. Born in the spring, right around the time the bluebonnets start coming up along the highway. You ever notice how they always grow thickest right there on the shoulder? I always thought it was the wind from the cars blowing the seeds around, but who knows.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms began in the context of a significant medical or neurological change, suggesting psychotic disorder due to another medical condition.
doctor.question: Did these experiences begin after any significant change in your health?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about 1 year and 5 months, since after my close friend passed away.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the onset of the experiences and whether they followed a specific event (like a health change). The 'duration' item explains that the symptoms started about 1 year and 5 months ago, following the passing of a close friend.

patient.answer:
Well, let's see... a change in my health? No, my health's been about the same. But I can tell you exactly when all this started. It's been about a year and five months now. Started right after my good friend Charlie passed away. Oh, Charlie... we knew each other since we were knee-high to a grasshopper. We used to go fishing down at Miller's Pond every single Saturday, rain or shine. He had this old aluminum johnboat that leaked just a little bit right near the transom. Not enough to sink you, but you had to keep a coffee tin handy to bail it out every hour or so. 

He always swore by those jitterbug lures. The green ones with the little yellow spots. Said the bass couldn't resist the sound they made popping across the top of the water. I always preferred a simple worm and bobber myself. There's something peaceful about just watching that red and white plastic bobbing out there, waiting for it to dip under. We'd sit out there for hours, drinking RC Cola and eating those little Debbie oatmeal cream pies. You know the ones? They used to be a lot bigger back in the day. Everything's getting smaller now, it seems. Even the candy bars at the checkout line. 

But yeah, it was right after Charlie's funeral that all this started up. About a year and five months ago. We buried him out at the Restland Cemetery, right near that big weeping willow tree. Beautiful spot, really. The shade keeps the grass nice and green all summer long.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms may be caused by an underlying neurological or medical condition.
doctor.question: Has a doctor ever told you that you have a neurological or brain condition?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about my medical history regarding neurological or brain conditions, which is not covered by my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
A brain condition? No, no sir. Never had any doctor tell me anything like that. I mean, old Doc Evans—he was the one who delivered half the county, you know—he did have to patch up my head once. But that was just a cut. Must've been... oh, the summer of '82, I reckon. I was working on the old John Deere combine out in the field. The green ones, you know? Not the big fancy machines they have now with the air-conditioned cabs and the satellite radios. Just a metal seat that'd burn the hide right off you if you left it sitting in the sun too long. You had to throw a burlap sack over it just to sit down. 

Anyway, I slipped off the ladder and whacked my head right on the hitch. Bled like a stuck pig. Head wounds always do, they say. Doc Evans put about eight stitches right here above my ear. He used this thick black thread, looked just like heavy-test fishing line. He always smelled like cherry pipe tobacco and rubbing alcohol, Doc Evans did. He'd smoke a corn cob pipe right there in the examination room while he was sewing you up! Can you imagine that today? They'd probably shut the whole clinic down for that now. But no, he never said nothing about my actual brain being bad. Just told me to keep the stitches clean and stay out of the midday sun for a spell.

doctor.intent: Assess for cognitive disorientation suggesting a medical or neurocognitive cause of the psychosis
doctor.question: Have you recently become confused about where you are?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about disorientation or confusion regarding location, which is not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Confused about where I am? No, I always know where I'm at. I've lived in this county my whole life, so there ain't a road or a dirt path I don't recognize. Even when they put in that new bypass over by the old Miller farm—you know the one, where they tore down that beautiful red barn? Such a shame, too. That barn was built back in the twenties. They used real wooden pegs instead of nails for the main beams. My daddy used to say a barn built with pegs would sway in a tornado but it wouldn't snap. 

I remember when we used to go out there to pick up hay. We'd stack those square bales so high on the flatbed you'd think the whole truck was gonna tip over going around a bend. You had to wear long sleeves, even in August, or that hay would scratch your arms up something awful. And the dust! You'd be sneezing for two days straight after hauling hay. We'd always stop at the filling station on the way back and get a cold bottle of Nehi Grape. Nothing tasted better than that cold grape soda after sweating in a hayfield all afternoon. But no, I don't get confused about where I am. I know exactly where I am.

doctor.intent: Assess for cognitive decline that could indicate an underlying neurocognitive or medical condition causing the psychosis.
doctor.question: Has your wife noticed any decline in your memory recently?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about memory decline, which is not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
My memory? No, she hasn't said anything about my memory slipping. Martha's usually pretty quick to point out if I forget something, like taking out the trash on Tuesday mornings. You know, the sanitation department changed their route a few years back. Used to be they'd come around on Thursdays, right about the time the mailman, Mr. Henderson, would drop off the post. 

Mr. Henderson was a real character. He had this little white mail truck with the steering wheel on the wrong side. He'd always leave a milk bone in the mailbox for our old golden retriever, Buster. Best dog we ever had, Buster was. We found him wandering near the old train tracks on the edge of town, just a skinny little pup. Took him in, fed him some leftover meatloaf, and he never left our side after that. He loved riding in the back of my pickup truck, just letting his ears flap in the wind. We had a '78 Ford F-150 back then. Two-tone, brown and tan. Had a manual transmission with the shifter right there on the steering column. Three on the tree, they called it. You don't see those much anymore. Everybody wants an automatic now, so they can hold their coffee in one hand and their telephone in the other while they drive. But no, Martha hasn't mentioned anything about my memory.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic experiences may be caused by an underlying medical or neurological condition.
doctor.question: Has a doctor found any medical or neurological condition that could explain these experiences?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about medical or neurological conditions that could explain the symptoms, which is a rule-out criterion not covered by the provided symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, no doctor has ever said anything like that. They haven't found any medical reason for what I go through. I mean, they did all sorts of blood tests a while back, taking vials and vials of it. The nurse who drew my blood, she was a sweet girl. Had hair the color of spun gold, just like my niece Sarah. 

Sarah used to come visit us every summer when she was little. We'd take her down to the creek to catch crawdads. You had to tie a piece of bacon to a string and just dangle it in the water, wait for them to pinch it. Then you'd scoop 'em up real quick with a net. We'd keep 'em in a galvanized bucket for a while, just to watch 'em, then toss 'em back. Sarah loved that. She's all grown up now, of course. Moved out to Seattle, works for one of those big computer companies. Sends us a Christmas card every year with a picture of her and her husband. They got a nice-looking house, big windows. But no, the doctors haven't found any physical sickness that would cause all this.

inference.note: Persistent delusions and hallucination-like experiences with preserved orientation and memory support F22 or late-onset F20.9. The patient reports no neurological disease, medical explanation, substance use, or cognitive decline, making F06.2 less likely.

doctor.intent: Determine whether he has prominent hallucinations beyond the persecutory/ referential beliefs, which would favor unspecified psychosis over delusional disorder.
doctor.question: Do you hear voices speaking to you when you are alone and there is no radio or other person nearby?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: Some afternoons, when the house is quiet, I hear my old friend call my name from the porch or hum a choir song, clear like he is standing right there.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I hear voices when no one is around, which directly addresses auditory hallucinations.

patient.answer:
Voices? Well, yes, sometimes I do. Some afternoons, when the house is real quiet and Martha's out at her garden club, I hear my old friend Jimmy. He'll call my name from the front porch, or I'll hear him humming one of those old choir songs, clear as day, like he's standing right there next to me. 

Jimmy had a beautiful baritone voice, you know. We used to sing in the church choir together back at First Methodist. The choir director, Mrs. Gable, she was a strict woman. Always wore these floral dresses with a lace collar and had her hair pinned up tight. If you missed a note, she'd tap her baton on the music stand so hard you'd think she was gonna snap it in two. But she knew how to get a good sound out of us. We did a Christmas cantata back in '65 that folks talked about for years. Jimmy had the solo on "O Holy Night." He hit that high note at the end and I swear the stained glass windows rattled just a little bit. 

Those windows were something else, too. They were imported all the way from Italy when the church was built. Had the whole story of the Good Samaritan in the big one facing the street. I remember sitting in the pew as a boy, just watching the sunlight come through that red glass in the Samaritan's robe. It would cast this pink glow right across the wooden pews. They don't make glass like that anymore, all hand-blown and pieced together with lead. Takes a real craftsman to do that kind of work. But yes, I hear Jimmy humming sometimes when I'm all alone.

doctor.intent: Assess for disorganized thought or behavior, which would favor an unspecified schizophrenia-spectrum psychotic disorder over delusional disorder.
doctor.question: Aside from the messages and voices, have you noticed yourself becoming unusually disorganized—for example, having trouble keeping your thoughts connected or behaving in ways that seem confusing to others?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: At domino games I have started tapping the tiles in the same pattern over and over and holding my hand up like I am stopping traffic, even though the others tell me to just play.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I have become unusually disorganized or behaved in ways that are confusing to others, which directly matches the symptom of disorganized or abnormal behavior.

patient.answer:
Disorganized? Well, I don't know if I'd call it that, but the fellas down at the lodge have been giving me a hard time lately. We play dominoes every Thursday afternoon, have for years. Lately, I guess I've been... well, I'll start tapping the tiles, you know? Just tapping them in this specific pattern, over and over. And sometimes I'll hold my hand up, kind of like a crossing guard stopping traffic, right in the middle of a hand. The guys will be telling me, "Come on, just play your tile," but I just... I have to do it that way. 

We play on this old felt-covered table that used to belong to Arthur Pendelton. Arthur was a character. He owned the hardware store on Main Street, the one that burned down back in '92. Terribly sad thing, that fire. Started in the back room where they kept the paint thinner. The fire department was there for hours, spraying water all over the place. The chief back then was a big burly fella named O'Malley. He had this magnificent mustache, curled right up at the ends. Used wax on it every morning, he told me once. He was always chewing on an unlit cigar, too. Said he promised his wife he'd quit smoking, so he just chewed on 'em instead. I don't know if that's any better for you, honestly. But yeah, the dominoes... the fellas get a little confused when I start tapping and holding my hand up like that.

inference.note: Persistent hallucinations and increasingly disorganized/repetitive behavior add support for schizophrenia-spectrum illness, while delusional disorder remains possible; no clear cognitive or medical cause identified.

doctor.intent: Determine whether hallucinations are prominent and independent of the delusional beliefs, which would favor schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis over delusional disorder.
doctor.question: Do you hear voices even when you are not thinking about the messages from the domino players or the radio?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the hallucinations (hearing voices) occur independently of the delusions (messages from the radio/domino players), which is a follow-up about the relationship between these psychotic symptoms rather than probing a new symptom profile or criteria.

patient.answer:
Well, I suppose I do... yes. The voices don't really care what I'm thinking about. I could be out on the porch, just watching the cars go by, not thinking about the dominoes or the radio at all, and Jimmy will still start humming. 

I was sitting out there just yesterday, actually. Watching Mr. Henderson's boy mow the lawn across the street. He uses one of those old push mowers, the kind with the spinning blades that go snick-snick-snick. It's good exercise for a boy his age. I had one just like it when I was a teenager. Used to cut grass all over the neighborhood for fifty cents a yard. Saved up enough to buy myself a genuine leather baseball mitt. The smell of that leather... there's nothing quite like it. I used to rub neat's-foot oil into it every night to keep it soft. Kept it under my mattress so it would form a perfect pocket. Played third base for the county league. We had a game against the boys from Oakhaven once, and I caught a line drive right down the third-base line that would've taken my head off if I hadn't put my glove up in time. The crowd went wild. My father was in the stands, wearing his good Sunday hat... but, what was I saying? Oh, right. No, the voices just come when they please, regardless of what's on my mind.

doctor.intent: Assess for disorganized speech, which would support schizophrenia over delusional disorder.
doctor.question: Have people told you recently that your speech is difficult to follow or that your thoughts seem to jump from one subject to another?

target_item.name: Racing_Thoughts
target_item.manifestation: My mind runs from the choir to baseball to repairs to my friend and back again so fast that I cannot hold one thought long enough to explain it right.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about my thoughts jumping from one subject to another and speech being difficult to follow, which corresponds to racing thoughts or flight of ideas.

patient.answer:
Well, my daughter Martha mentioned something about that just the other morning over breakfast. She said she couldn't keep up with what I was saying. But it's just... my mind runs from the choir to baseball to repairs to my friend Jimmy and back again so fast that I cannot hold one thought long enough to explain it right. 

Speaking of repairs, I was looking at the hinges on our screen door yesterday and they are getting awful rusty. You have to keep those oiled or they'll squeak every time the wind blows. My father used to keep a little can of 3-in-One oil on the top shelf in the mudroom just for things like that. That mudroom always smelled like wet wool and machine oil. We had this big old sheepdog named Barnaby who used to sleep out there on an old braided rug. Best dog you could ever ask for, though he had a terrible habit of chasing the mailman. 

The mail carrier back then was a fella named Mr. Higgins. He wore this smart little gray uniform with a cap, and he always kept a pocketful of dog biscuits to keep Barnaby at bay. Higgins had a bit of a limp from the war, you know. Served over in the Pacific. He brought back a real Japanese compass and showed it to me once when I was a boy... but, yes, I suppose my thoughts do jump around a bit too fast for folks to follow sometimes.

inference.note: This turn added prominent disorganized speech and repetitive/odd behaviors, with late-life onset raising concern for an unspecified major neurocognitive disorder; persistent hallucinations and delusions remain compatible with F20.9 or F22.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms are associated with a progressive decline in cognitive functioning, which would support major neurocognitive disorder over a primary psychotic disorder.
doctor.question: Have you had trouble managing tasks you used to handle independently, such as paying bills, taking medications, or getting dressed?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I have missed choir rehearsals, let parts of my garden go, and made the domino games uncomfortable enough that I do not join like I used to.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulties managing daily tasks and activities, which corresponds to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Well, managing things... I suppose some things have slipped a bit. I haven't been going to choir rehearsals lately, which is a shame. And I've let parts of my garden go to weed. Plus, like I said, I've made the domino games uncomfortable enough that I just don't join in like I used to. 

I used to grow the most beautiful prize-winning tomatoes in that garden. Big, juicy Beefsteaks. My wife, Lord rest her soul, used to make the most wonderful tomato preserves. People think tomato preserves sound strange, but you put a little ginger and lemon in there, and it's just delightful on a piece of toast. We had this old toaster, a heavy chrome thing that you had to flip the sides down to turn the bread. You had to watch it like a hawk or it would burn your toast to a crisp. My brother Henry burned a piece so bad once, it set off the smoke alarm and the fire department came. It wasn't O'Malley that time, though, it was a younger fellow... but yes, I guess I haven't been keeping up with things as well as I should.

inference.note: Prominent hallucinations, disorganized speech/behavior, and functional decline make delusional disorder (F22) less likely; dementia with behavioral disturbance/psychosis (F03.91) is now more consistent than F03.90.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is cognitive decline causing loss of independent functioning, which would favor dementia with psychosis over schizophrenia.
doctor.question: Who currently manages the household bills, and has that responsibility changed from how it was handled before these symptoms began?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking a specific follow-up question about who manages the household bills, which is not covered in the patient's symptom profile (the functional impairment manifestation only mentions choir rehearsals, the garden, and domino games).

patient.answer:
Well, the bills... Martha handles all of that now. My daughter, Martha. She took over the checkbook a few months back. I used to do it all myself, you know. Every Friday evening, I'd sit down at the kitchen table with my ledger and a good, sharp pencil. 

I always liked the yellow Ticonderoga pencils. The eraser on those is just the right kind of rubber, doesn't smudge the paper when you make a mistake. My father taught me to keep my pencils sharp with a pocketknife. He had this little bone-handled Case knife he carried everywhere. Used it to whittle little wooden whistles out of willow branches for me and Henry when we were boys. You have to get the willow in the spring when the sap is running, or the bark won't slip off right to make the air chamber. Henry was always better at making them than I was. He could get a real high, clear note out of his, while mine always sounded a bit airy. Henry ended up playing the trumpet in the high school marching band, actually. They had these maroon uniforms with gold braiding on the shoulders. He looked so sharp marching down Main Street in the Fourth of July parade... but, oh, what were we talking about? The bills. Yes, Martha pays them now. I just couldn't keep the numbers straight anymore.

doctor.intent: Determine whether cognitive and functional decline began before the psychotic symptoms
doctor.question: Before you began hearing voices and receiving messages, had you already been having a gradual decline in your memory or ability to manage everyday tasks?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a gradual decline in memory or functioning prior to the onset of psychotic symptoms (likely to rule out dementia), which is not explicitly covered in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, no, not really. Before all that business with the voices and the messages started, I was doing just fine. My memory was sharp as a tack. I remember the exact day the messages started coming through the radio, actually. We have this little silver radio in the kitchen. Not like the old Philco we had when I was a boy. Now that was a real radio. Beautiful wooden cabinet, took up half the parlor. My father bought it back in... oh, must have been 1938 or so. 

We used to sit around it on Sunday nights and listen to Jack Benny. He was such a funny man. We'd have popcorn, too. Mother would pop it right on the stove in a heavy cast-iron skillet with a bit of bacon grease. You just don't get popcorn that tastes like that from those microwave bags they have nowadays. The bags always leave a funny waxy coating on the roof of your mouth. Martha buys those bags for her kids, and I tell her, 'Martha, just use a pan!' But everybody is in such a rush these days. Rush, rush, rush... wait, what was it you asked me? Did you want to know about the radio?

inference.note: New information supports a major neurocognitive disorder with behavioral disturbance: progressive functional decline, impaired financial management, disorganized speech, hallucinations, and delusions. Primary schizophrenia remains possible but is less likely given late onset and cognitive decline.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there was a longstanding psychotic disorder predating the recent cognitive and functional changes.
doctor.question: Before the past year or so, had you ever heard voices or believed that other people were sending you special messages?

target_item.name: Psychotic Symptoms Duration
target_item.manifestation: The voices and special messages have been happening on and off for about 9 months now.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the onset and duration of the psychotic symptoms (hearing voices and receiving special messages).

patient.answer:
Well, no, never before. It's really just been happening on and off for about 9 months now. Nine months... so that means it started right around the end of the summer. We had a terrible heatwave late last August, just baked the ground solid. It was so hot the tar on the county roads was getting soft and sticking to the tires of my old Ford pickup. 

That truck was a 1974 F-150, powder blue. Best vehicle I ever owned. Had a three-on-the-tree manual transmission. You don't see those anymore. Kids today wouldn't know how to shift a gear if their lives depended on it. Everything is automatic now. Automatic cars, automatic coffee makers... I remember when you had to percolate coffee on the stove. It made that wonderful bubbling sound, and the whole house would smell like roasting beans. My mother used to buy the Eight O'Clock coffee from the A&P store down the road. They'd grind it right there at the checkout counter, and the cashier, Mrs. Gable, she always gave me a piece of peppermint candy. The bag of coffee had this little metal tie at the top to keep it fresh, and I used to save those ties to fix things around the house... but, what did you ask me? Did you want to know about the truck? Oh, the voices. Yes, no, it hasn't been forever. Just the last nine months or so.

inference.note: Added evidence of disorganized speech, repetitive behaviors, and loss of instrumental functioning, supporting a neurocognitive disorder with behavioral disturbance; late onset and functional decline make primary schizophrenia less likely but it remains a differential.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether there is objective recent-memory decline consistent with a neurocognitive disorder.
doctor.question: Has your daughter noticed that you forget recent events or conversations?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about memory loss or forgetfulness, which is not covered by the patient's symptom profile (Schizoaffective Disorder, Bipolar Type).

patient.answer:
Well, no, I don't think Martha's said anything about me forgetting things. We talk every morning, actually. She calls me right at eight o'clock when she's driving the kids to school. She's got this big minivan now, one of those ones where the doors slide open by themselves if you just push a button on the keys. 

I don't know how I feel about all these buttons and computers in cars. Back when I got my first car, it was a 1952 Chevrolet Bel Air. Had this beautiful chrome grille that looked like a big smile. I used to spend every Saturday morning out in the driveway, just polishing that chrome until you could see your reflection in it clear as day. Used Turtle Wax, the kind that came in the little green tub. You had to rub it on, let it dry to a haze, and then buff it off with a soft cloth. I always used my old flannel shirts for buffing once they got too threadbare to wear. They were the best for not scratching the paint. My wife, Helen, God rest her soul, she used to get so mad at me because I'd be out there fussing with the car instead of helping her in the garden. She grew the most beautiful tomatoes, big red Beefsteaks. We'd slice them thick, put a little salt and pepper on them, and eat them right on white bread with mayonnaise... but, oh, what was it you were asking? Did you want to know about the tomatoes? No, wait... about Martha? Yeah, she hasn't mentioned me forgetting things.

inference.note: The absence of a clear progressive memory decline before psychosis, together with prominent hallucinations, referential delusions, disorganized speech, and disorganized behavior, favors late-onset schizophrenia over unspecified dementia.

opening_question.question: Hello, it’s nice to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: Persistent psychotic symptoms for approximately nine months, including referential/persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations, disorganized speech, and odd/disorganized behavior, with clear social and instrumental functional decline. The patient denies substance use and reports no known medical or neurological cause. Duration is inconsistent with brief psychotic disorder; cognitive decline is not clearly established, making unspecified schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis the best-supported diagnosis.

Believes radio announcers are delivering messages specifically intended for him.
Confronts others because of these perceived messages.
Hears voices and messages when no person or radio source is present.
Hears his deceased friend Jimmy call his name and hum choir songs.
Reports voices occurring independently of his thoughts about the messages.
Speech is difficult for family members to follow.
Thoughts rapidly jump between unrelated topics.
Frequently loses track of the question or topic being discussed.
Repeatedly taps domino tiles in a specific pattern during games.
Raises and holds his hand in an unusual manner during domino games despite others prompting him to continue.
Stopped attending longstanding choir rehearsals because he cannot focus.
Has allowed parts of his garden to become overgrown.
Stopped participating in longstanding domino games because of conflict related to his beliefs.
Transferred management of household bills and the checkbook to his daughter because he could no longer keep the numbers straight.

diagnostic_checklist.duration_verified: Psychotic symptoms were reported for approximately nine months, with onset within the past year and persistence on and off during that period.
additional_requirements: At least one core psychotic symptom is explicitly present: delusions and auditory hallucinations.
Duration exceeds one month and is reported to exceed six months.
Clinically significant social and instrumental functional decline is confirmed.
Patient reports no known medical or neurological condition explaining the symptoms.
No clear major mood episode is described.
Cognitive decline preceding psychosis is denied or not established.
